speaker: Steven Strogatz
title: Steven Strogatz on the Humanity of Math | 3b1b Podcast
question: In frontier mathematics, why do AI systems outperform humans at problem-solving yet underperform at theory-building?
guest: Right now, the AIs are not good at asking questions. We're seeing this in math at the frontier: they are not inventing new theories. We make this distinction between problem-solving and theory building. They've shown themselves to be superhuman in problem-solving, and subhuman compared to the very best in theory building. No surprise—they're not trained to do that. I've tried to get them to make up test questions for my complex analysis exam. They were competent and pedestrian, like any textbook—very routine, not juicy questions that would challenge my best students. Though as a heuristic, if an exam question is too interesting to the professor, it's usually too hard for students under pressure. In research math, they're so far not very good at building new concepts because we haven't trained them to ask questions; we've trained them to answer questions. Taste, asking good questions, and building theory are teachable skills, though very few people know how to teach the art of discovery.

points.core: Training pipelines optimize models to answer existing questions rather than pose new ones.
points.note: Accept: reinforcement learning, benchmarks, or training objectives reward solving well-posed problems instead of formulating conjectures or inventing concepts. Do not credit: vague claims that AI lacks consciousness or true intelligence.

points.core: AI-generated mathematical questions default to competent textbook routines instead of surprising challenges.
points.note: Accept: models produce pedestrian, standard, or derivative prompts rather than juicy, novel, or concept-generating questions. Do not credit: claiming AI questions are completely broken or mathematically invalid.

points.core: Human mentors rarely formalize how to teach the art of mathematical discovery.
points.note: Accept: theory-building, taste, or question-asking are hard-to-codify skills that even few human professors know how to teach explicitly, making them harder to train into models. Do not credit: claiming discovery is permanently unteachable without acknowledging the formalization gap.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The premise is only partly true: AI now matches or beats most humans on well-posed problems (olympiad questions, benchmark-style research problems, some open conjectures), but top mathematicians still outperform it on many hard open problems. The asymmetry is real, though, and it has a few causes.

Problem-solving has a clear target and a checkable answer. A proof can be verified, often formally in Lean, so systems can search at enormous scale, get reliable feedback, and train on it. They also draw on a breadth of known techniques that no single human can match.

Theory-building lacks all of that. There is no objective signal for a "good" definition or a fruitful conjecture; value is a matter of taste and is judged over decades by a community. Training data is sparse, because papers record polished results rather than the exploratory process that produced the concepts. It also requires sustained coherence over years and a willingness to depart from existing frameworks, whereas current models are strongest at recombining what already exists.

In short, AI excels where success is verifiable and searchable, and lags where the goal itself must be invented.

points.why: The response explains that verifiable solutions provide reliable training feedback, while proposing fruitful conjectures or definitions lacks a comparable signal.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Problem-solving in mathematics gives AI systems what they exploit best: fixed definitions, explicit rules, and an unambiguous target, whether a tighter bound or a formal proof checkable in Lean. Because correctness is automatically verifiable, models can train via reinforcement learning on crisp reward signals and deploy massive test-time search, rapidly recombining vast repertoires of known techniques across enormous deduction spaces where human working memory bottlenecks.

Theory-building, by contrast, is open-ended and lacks an immediate objective function. Rather than proving a stated claim within an established language, it requires inventing the right definitions, abstractions, and conjectures to unify disparate phenomena and simplify whole classes of future questions. Judging whether a new concept is genuinely fruitful demands mathematical taste, cross-domain intuition, and long-horizon research judgment whose payoff emerges only through downstream discoveries. Moreover, mathematical corpora record polished theorems rather than the messy, iterative conceptual revisions that birth new frameworks, leaving AI formidable at tactical deduction inside existing paradigms yet weak at conceiving new ones.

points.why: The response explains why training rewards solving well-posed problems more readily than formulating new conjectures or concepts.
quotes: Because correctness is automatically verifiable, models can train via reinforcement learning on crisp reward signals
Theory-building, by contrast, is open-ended and lacks an immediate objective function.

The response identifies gaps in mathematical corpora but does not say that few human mentors know how to teach discovery explicitly.

noweb.answer:
Mathematical problem-solving operates within a fixed conceptual framework: definitions, axioms, and the target claim are already specified, providing a clear, verifiable objective. Paired with formal proof assistants and automated verifiers, proving a theorem becomes a bounded search problem. AI systems excel here because they can explore vast combinatorial spaces, draw on millions of learned proof tactics, and apply reinforcement learning against unambiguous pass-or-fail feedback at superhuman scale.

Theory-building, by contrast, lacks a predefined target or crisp reward signal. Instead of finding a logical path between fixed points, it requires inventing the conceptual landscape itself—crafting new definitions, abstractions, and conjectures that unify disparate phenomena and dissolve hard problems by reframing them. Judging whether a new abstraction is deep or fruitful depends on mathematical taste, cross-domain analogy, explanatory compression, and sparse historical precedent, where training data is scarce and verification is delayed by years of downstream inquiry. Because current AI thrives on optimizing explicit objectives rather than evaluating open-ended conceptual worth, it dominates tactical deduction within existing theories while struggling to originate them.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The premise is only partly true. By late 2026 AI systems match or beat most humans on hard problems with clear answers, such as olympiad problems, FrontierMath-style benchmarks and some open conjectures. They do not yet beat the best research mathematicians across the board. Still, the gap is real, and it mostly comes down to how each activity can be trained and checked.

Problem-solving has a fixed target and a checkable result: a number, a proof or a Lean certificate. That lets developers use reinforcement learning against automatic verifiers, generate huge amounts of synthetic practice, and run wide searches. Those are all areas where machines have the advantage.

Theory-building has no such reward signal. It means deciding which questions are worth asking, inventing definitions and abstractions, and judging whether a framework will pay off across many future results. Grothendieck's schemes are an example. The value of that work shows up only over years, through how the community uses it, so there's no quick verifier to train against.

Training data is also thin. Papers show polished results, not the false starts and reframing that produced them, and good taste is mostly passed on informally. So current systems are strong at search inside a given framework and weak at reshaping the framework itself. That's an inference from how they're trained, not a settled finding.

Problem-solving in frontier mathematics operates within an established framework where goals are well-defined and solutions can be objectively verified, often mechanically through proof assistants. This structure plays directly to AI strengths: models can combine broad cross-literature pattern recognition with massive test-time search and reinforcement learning to uncover intricate arguments, constructions, or counterexamples that outpace human endurance.

Theory-building, by contrast, is fundamentally open-ended and lacks an objective reward signal. It requires choosing which questions matter, inventing definitions that isolate the right underlying structure, and formulating unifying abstractions whose payoff may only become clear years later. Because no automated verifier can judge whether a new concept is fertile, illuminating, or natural, optimization-driven systems struggle to navigate the vast space of logically valid but sterile definitions. Until AI develops genuine mathematical taste—the long-horizon judgment to recognize deep analogies and compress complexity into conceptual frameworks that reshape how mathematicians think—it will remain far stronger at navigating existing landscapes than redrawing the map.

noweb.answer:
In frontier mathematics, problem-solving provides a fixed target and an objective verifier, creating an ideal arena for AI. Once a conjecture is stated, systems can exploit formal proof checkers, massive tree search, and reinforcement learning to navigate vast deductive spaces and uncover intricate proof paths that humans might miss.

Theory-building, by contrast, is fundamentally open-ended and lacks a clean reward signal. Rather than proving a given claim, it demands deciding which questions are worth asking, inventing the right definitions, and recognizing deep structural analogies across seemingly unrelated domains. A great theory does not merely generate true statements; it compresses complexity, reframes confusion into clarity, and creates conceptual tools that remain fertile for decades. Because there is no automated test for whether a new abstraction is genuinely illuminating rather than technically valid yet sterile, theory-building relies heavily on mathematical taste, semantic grounding, and long-horizon judgment—capacities that current optimization-driven AI systems still struggle to replicate.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
AI systems can outperform humans on some hard, well-specified math problems because they can explore many candidate approaches quickly. A fixed statement gives the search a target, and when a proof can be checked automatically, the system gets a clear signal of success.

Theory-building requires choosing the targets. A mathematician has to decide which patterns deserve an explanation, which definitions capture the right structure, and which conjectures could connect results that seem unrelated. A proof can certify a theorem, but there’s no comparable test for whether a new definition will make an entire area easier to understand. That judgment often takes years of seeing what the ideas explain and what new questions they open up. Current AI systems have much stronger feedback for finding proofs than for making those choices.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
The gap is clearest on well-specified problems. AI systems can outperform expert mathematicians on some frontier tasks, but frontier problem-solving as a whole is too varied for a blanket comparison. Given a precise conjecture, a system can explore many proof strategies quickly. Where a proof checker is available, it can also get reliable feedback on each attempted step.

Theory-building requires choosing the questions and sometimes inventing the language in which to ask them. A new definition can be perfectly consistent yet explain little. Its value may become apparent only when it unifies seemingly unrelated results or makes a previously inaccessible problem tractable. Human mathematicians draw on years of partial results, failed approaches, and examples to judge which ideas deserve sustained attention. AI can propose definitions and conjectures too. The harder task is recognizing which ones will matter when there is no agreed target and the strongest evidence of their value may arrive years later.
